ety.text: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ed- (“grain, barley”). The term may derive from Proto-Italic *adōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd-ōs (“dried stuff, grain”, collective). Alternatively, it may derive from Proto-Italic *ados, from *h₂éd-os, perhaps whence also Old Irish ad, Gothic 𐌰𐍄𐌹𐍃𐌺 (atisk), and Old Armenian հատ (hat). Hittite [script needed] (ḫattar) has also been connected, though this is highly uncertain.

ety.text: From Proto-Italic *klaudtrom, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂ud- (“key, hook, nail”) + *-trom (“instrumental suffix”). Equivalent to claud- (“to close, enclose”) + -trum. Related to Latin clāvis (“key”), clāvus (“nail, peg”), claustra (“dam, wall, barricade, stronghold”). Cognate with Ancient Greek κλείς (kleís, “bar, bolt, key”), Old High German slioȥan (“to close, conclude, lock”), Old Saxon slūtan (“to close, conclude, lock”).

From suī (genitive reflexive pronoun) + -cīdium (“act of killing or murder”). Its use in modern Romance languages and New Latin is attested later than, and perhaps ultimately from, English suicide. Suicida (“self-killer”), from suī + -cīda (“killer”), is attested in Walter of Saint Victor's Contra quatuor labyrinthos Franciae (c. 1177), but both suicidium and suicida were otherwise unfound throughout the Middle Ages.
